title: Goal-Oriented Ordered Autoencoding for Successive Refinement in Progressive Communication
authors: Qi Liao; Dario Bega
abstract: Goal-oriented communication often struggles to sustain downstream task performance under variable and unpredictable bandwidth. We address this problem by proposing GO-OAE (Goal-Oriented Ordered AutoEncoding), which learns a progressively refinable quantized latent sequence, optimized directly for task utility rather than source reconstruction. Each component of the sequence is represented for transmission by its code index, and the learned ordering enables inference from any received prefix of the index sequence, with performance improving as more indices arrive. We prove that optimizing the goal-oriented distortion objective is equivalent to solving a weighted conditional information bottleneck formulation, and introduce an unbiased multi-prefix importance sampling (MPIS) estimator, to reduce GO-OAE training computational cost from O(BK) to O(Bm) with m << K, and reduces the estimator variance by a factor of 1/m. Experiments show that, on MiniImageNet, GO-OAE achieves over 96% of the lossless upper-bound classification accuracy using 324 bits per image (683X compression vs. raw RGB), and already attains over 94% of the upper bound with only 70% of the transmitted indices. It consistently outperforms reconstruction-optimized codecs and ordered autoencoders trained with uniform prefix sampling across all transmission budgets, demonstrating effective communication at extreme compression rates.

title: Algorithmic Justice and Responsible AI Journalism: A Comparative Communication Policy Perspective in East Asia
authors: Renxiudi Huang; Linjia Bai
abstract: As generative artificial intelligence and automated content curation rapidly reshape the global media landscape, the intersection of algorithmic justice and media governance has become a critical frontier for sustainable development. This study provides a comparative communication policy analysis of China and South Korea, focusing explicitly on how their distinct regulatory toolkits address the tension between algorithmic fairness and platform accountability in AI journalism. While China utilizes a top-down, state-centric regulatory framework emphasizing ideological security, algorithmic registration, and strict synthetic media labeling, South Korea employs a multi-stakeholder co-regulation model driven by personal data protection, anti-monopoly platform intervention, and civil society oversight. Through a detailed textual analysis of key policy documents—including China's Provisions on the Administration of Algorithmic Recommendations and South Korea's Guidelines for AI Service Ethics to Protect Users—alongside empirical evidence from prominent algorithmic news curation platforms (Toutiao and Naver), this paper evaluates the implementation efficacy and structural trade-offs of each nation's approach. We demonstrate that while both models mitigate the risks of digital infodemics and algorithmic bias, they face contrasting trade-offs between regulatory efficiency and editorial independence. Finally, this study introduces the "Policy-Media-Society" (PMS) responsive governance framework, clarifying how systemic institutional adaptations can advance UN Sustainable Development Goal 16 (SDG 16) by ensuring public access to transparent, verified information.

title: Krum-Inspired Central Teacher Selection and Residual Channel Bottlenecks for Efficient DeepSC
authors: Rami Eid; Mostafa Jammoul; Omar Kaaki; Maria Slim; Mariette Awad; Hadi Sarieddeen
abstract: Deploying transformer-based semantic communication models on edge devices requires compression that preserves semantic fidelity under channel variability. We study a compressed deep semantic communication (DeepSC) student trained by multi-teacher knowledge distillation and combine two ideas: (i) a residual channel bottleneck that splits the transmitted representation into a base stream and a residual stream with unequal power allocation, and (ii) a Krum-inspired, medoid-style centrality criterion that selects a single central teacher from a five-model ensemble, applied at the logit and intermediate-feature levels and combined with a feature-dominant distillation loss. On the EuroParl benchmark, a two-layer student recovers about 98% of the four-layer teacher's bilingual evaluation understudy (BLEU)-1 under additive white Gaussian noise, with 93% of its BLEU-4 and 96% of its sentence-BERT (SBERT) score, and about 89%, 77%, and 87% of the teacher's BLEU-1, BLEU-4, and SBERT, respectively, under Rayleigh fading, while reducing non-embedding parameters by 1.33x and single-teacher inference latency by 1.79x (9.0x relative to a five-teacher ensemble used here as an upper-bound reference, not a deployment baseline). Controlled ablations over three seeds indicate complementary contributions of about +8.4% BLEU-1 (+9.6% SBERT) from the residual bottleneck and +3.0% (+2.9% SBERT) from centrality-based selection over mean aggregation. A decoder-mode ablation shows that the base stream alone recovers about two-thirds of the full BLEU-1 while the residual stream alone collapses, supporting the role of the residual as a refinement on top of the base.

title: Where to Defend? Layer-Wise Adversarial Training for Robust Transformer-Based Semantic Communications
authors: Maria Slim; Razane Tajeddine; Mariette Awad; Hadi Sarieddeen
abstract: Deep learning-based semantic communication (DeepSC), a Transformer-based encoder-decoder, achieves semantic fidelity over noisy channels but remains vulnerable to adversarial perturbations injected at multiple stages of the pipeline. We present a layer-wise robustness framework that compares fast gradient sign method (FGSM), projected gradient descent (PGD), and l2-normalized fast gradient method (FGM) defenses at the embedding output, and then uses PGD to analyze three attack and defense points: the embedding output, encoder output, and channel-encoder bottleneck. We evaluate reconstruction on Europarl and UK Hansard and sentiment classification on SST2 and YELP under additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) and Rayleigh fading. A first-order damage budget, {epsilon} times the l1 norm of the clean-input loss gradient at each injection point, predicts the attack-severity ordering, and the transfer matrix reveals asymmetric defense transfer: the embedding defense transfers strongly to encoder attacks, whereas encoder defenses degrade robustness against upstream attacks. For reconstruction, encoder-point training yields the largest matched gain but fails severely under embedding attacks; joint embedding-plus-encoder training retains comparable gains under encoder attacks while mitigating this mismatch failure, and Rayleigh fading attenuates robustness gains and degradation. For classification, three of four defenses collapse to constant predictors; only the channel-encoder defense remains non-degenerate, suggesting a protective role for the 128D-to-16D bottleneck. At a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 9 dB and perturbation budget {epsilon} = 0.3, the matched encoder defense recovers bilingual evaluation understudy (BLEU) from ~ 0.10 to ~ 0.64 on Europarl/AWGN, whereas the mismatched encoder defense yields a -0.444 BLEU change relative to the undefended baseline under an embedding attack.

title: Semantic-Aware Sub-Band Allocation for Terahertz Communications
authors: Fatima Ismail; Hadi Sarieddeen; Jihad Fahs
abstract: This paper studies semantic-aware sub-band al- location for terahertz (THz) communication systems, where frequency-selective molecular absorption creates highly non- uniform sub-band qualities. Unlike conventional formulations, semantic fidelity depends nonlinearly on the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and is also sentence-specific, leading to a non-separable assignment problem that is generally not solvable using simple ordering-based policies. To address this, we use a sentence-BERT (SBERT)-based surrogate model that predicts semantic fidelity from the sentence embedding and sub-band SNR. We propose an importance-aware scheduler that assigns sentences to sub- bands based on their semantic contribution using an oracle utility function that captures importance-weighted semantic similarity across sentence-sub-band pairs. A neural scheduler is then trained through imitation learning to approximate the oracle policy at more than 200x lower runtime than full DeepSC- based oracle evaluation. Integrated with a deep-learning-enabled semantic communication (DeepSC) system, the proposed method consistently outperforms all benchmark schemes and approaches oracle-level performance under realistic THz channel conditions.

title: Flexible Deep Joint Source-Channel Coding: A Vibrotactile Example
authors: Shuijie Li; Kemi Chen; Runjie Wang; Tiesong Zhao; Xiaoming Tao
abstract: The increasing demand for real-time tactile communication in multimedia systems has exposed the limitations of existing Joint Source-Channel Coding (JSCC) techniques. While current JSCC models facilitate end-to-end optimization, they typically operate at fixed coding rates and require separate model instances for different rate settings. This results in significant storage overhead and limited adaptability to dynamic bandwidth conditions. To address these challenges, we propose the Flexible Deep Joint Source-Channel Coding (FD-JSCC) framework for vibrotactile signals, which supports flexible-rate transmission without the need for model switching. The FD-JSCC integrates a flexible-rate encoder-decoder enhanced with Hierarchical Gain Adaptation Module (HGAM) and Rate-Switchable Residual Module (RSRM), enabling bitrate-aware compression by selectively preserving salient vibrotactile features. Additionally, we introduce a Channel Feature Processing Module (CFPM), which leverages real-time SNR information to enhance robustness against channel noise and signal degradation. Trained on the IEEE 1918.1.1 vibrotactile dataset, FD-JSCC achieves reconstruction performance comparable to fixed-rate baselines (e.g., DeepSC-S), while reducing storage requirements by 61.1\% when supporting four rates. These results underscore its potential for scalable, low-latency tactile communication in next-generation networks.

title: Compressibility is not Feedback: A Random-access Gap in Causal Semantic Repair
authors: Milad Bafarassat
abstract: Semantic feedback can repair a noisy first decode without retransmitting the whole message, but current end-to-end evaluations hide where a feedback design fails. An oracle that sees both the source-side state and receiver observation may describe a useful correction with few bits, while the receiver, which sees only its own observation, may not know which correction to request. We formulate these as distinct direct and receiver-constrained coding problems, connect repair distortion to retained local utility and prove a random-access separation: one direct bit is exact although receiver utility vanishes with the number of source-conditioned alternatives. A synthetic ladder verifies the exact law. In paired populations of eight Reuters text-JSCC codecs, the trained recurrent population retains over three times more direct 16-bit repair value than the trained DeepSC population despite comparable full-repair opportunity. Nevertheless, an entropy-valid receiver audit across all eight recurrent checkpoints does not resolve against repetition, source-only or shuffled-index controls. The results show that compressible repair is an upper bound, not evidence of deployable feedback, and motivate reporting both rate curves under matched resources.

title: SignDeepSC: A Semantic Signature-based Approach for Robust Semantic Communication
authors: Khalil Alhaj; Razane Tajeddine; Hadi Sarieddeen
abstract: Semantic communication systems such as deep semantic communication (DeepSC) offer high efficiency but are vulnerable to adversarial attacks on their underlying neural networks. We address a physical-layer man-in-the-middle (MitM) threat in which an adversary injects perturbations into the transmitted signal to distort its meaning. We propose SignDeepSC, an architectural defense that achieves adversarial robustness without requiring explicit adversarial example generation during training. The approach is built on a perceiver-inspired semantic signature, a compact vector summary of the source features transmitted over a separate low-rate auxiliary channel. This signature is used by a self-repairing decoder that leverages cross-attention to correct distortions and can additionally drive a scrambler that shuffles the feature layout. We evaluate SignDeepSC over Rayleigh fading and additive white Gaussian noise channels under both single-step fast gradient sign method (FGSM) and iterative projected gradient descent (PGD) attacks. Under PGD ($ε= 0.7$), at 12~dB signal-to-noise ratio with Rayleigh fading, SignDeepSC achieves a bilingual evaluation understudy (BLEU-4) score of 0.237 and bidirectional encoder representations from transformers (BERT) sentence similarity of 0.646, outperforming all baselines without degrading clean-channel performance, when the signature channel is well protected.

title: Structured Spectral Compression based Low-Bitrate Secure Speech Communications for Internet of Things assisted Non-Terrestrial Networks
authors: Li Ping Qian; Zhehan Chen; Qianru Wang; Qian Wang; Yuan Wu; Xuemin Sherman Shen
abstract: This paper focuses on the Low-Bitrate Secure Speech Communications based on the Structured Spectral Compression (LB-S2C2). Specifically, the Mel spectral matrix of the speech signal is first encoded at the transmitter side through compressive sensing based on waveform segmentation and data quantization. Then, the Automatic Repeat Request (ARQ) is combined with forward error correction to achieve reliable transmission of speech signals over wireless channels. Thirdly, the received signals are recovered as the speech at the receiver side. Finally, we conduct a series of simulation experiments for the performance evaluation of LB-S2C2. Our simulations reveal that the dictionary matrix used for the speech reconstruction is different from the one used for the high-order matrix sparsification by even only approximately 0.1%, and then the accurate speech recovery fails. It implies that the speech data can be securely transmitted when the dictionary matrix is preserved. More importantly, the LB-S2C2 exhibits a very high privacy protection capability with the average voiceprint similarity to be only 0.3, which is much lower than the 0.8 of the semantic speech communication scheme DeepSC-S, and even lower than the 0.33 of the latest speech communication scheme OFI-OFCNB. In addition, our simulations reveal that the proposed structured speech coding boasts a time complexity of merely O(n), and the proposed speech recovery scheme requires the 12-bit memory storage only, which outperforms the traditional encryption algorithms proposed for speech communications. In comparison with the conventional compression techniques, our spectral compression method renders the coding rate of only 3.9kbps, which is lower than the current lowest speech coding rate of 6.3kbps achieved by G.723.

title: Semantic Communications in the THz Band
authors: Fatima Ismail; Hadi Sarieddeen; Jihad Fahs
abstract: Semantic and terahertz (THz)-band communications are algorithmic and spectral enablers of future wireless networks. This work investigates deep learning-based semantic communication (DeepSC) over THz channels. We show that DeepSC models trained solely under additive white Gaussian noise generalize well to the tested THz block- and fast-fading channels when receiver-side compensation is applied. To enable fully data-driven reception, we propose a lightweight neural detector that does not require channel state information (CSI). At 0.3 THz, DeepSC outperforms a throughput-matched traditional coded communication system baseline over 0-12 dB signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), achieving more than 50 percentage-point higher Bilingual Evaluation Understudy unigram (BLEU-1) score. The proposed pilot-free detector outperforms minimum mean square error (MMSE) equalization with both perfect and imperfect CSI and remains robust to frequency offsets up to 50 MHz, highlighting the resilience of semantic communication to THz channel impairments.

title: Image Semantic Communication with Quadtree Partition-based Coding
authors: Yinhuan Huang; Zhijin Qin
abstract: Deep learning based semantic communication (DeepSC) system has emerged as a promising paradigm for efficient wireless transmission. However, existing image DeepSC methods, frequently encounter challenges in balancing rate-distortion performance and computational complexity, and often exhibit inferior performance compared to traditional schemes, especially on high-resolution datasets. To address these limitations, we propose a novel image DeepSC system, using quadtree partition-based joint semantic-channel coding, named Quad-DeepSC, which maintains low complexity while achieving state-of-the-art transmission performance. Based on maturing learned image compression technologies, we establish a unified DeepSC system design and training pipeline. The proposed Quad-DeepSC integrates quadtree partition-based entropy estimation and feature coding modules with lightweight feature extraction and reconstruction networks to form an end-to-end architecture. During training, all components except the feature coding modules are jointly optimized as a compact learned image codec, Quad-LIC, for source compression tasks. The pretrained Quad-LIC is then embedded into Quad-DeepSC and fine-tuned end-to-end over wireless channels. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that Quad-DeepSC is the first DeepSC system to surpass conventional communication systems, which employ VTM for source coding and adopt the optimal MCS index under 3GPP standards for channel coding and digital modulation, in performance across datasets of varying resolutions. Notably, both Quad-DeepSC and Quad-LIC exhibit minimal latency, rendering them well-suited for deployment in real-time wireless communication systems.

title: VQ-VAE Based Digital Semantic Communication with Importance-Aware OFDM Transmission
authors: Ming Lyu; Hao Chen; Dan Wang; Chen Qiu; Guangyin Feng; Nan Ma; Xiaodong Xu
abstract: Semantic communication (SemCom) significantly reduces redundant data and improves transmission efficiency by extracting the latent features of information. However, most of the conventional deep learning-based SemCom systems focus on analog transmission and lack in compatibility with practical digital communications. This paper proposes a vector quantized-variational autoencoder (VQ-VAE) based digital SemCom system that directly transmits the semantic features and incorporates the importance-aware orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) transmission to enhance the SemCom performance, where the VQ-VAE generates a discrete codebook shared between the transmitter and receiver. At transmitter, the latent semantic features are firstly extracted by VQ-VAE, and then the shared codebook is adopted to match these features, which are subsequently transformed into a discrete version to adapt the digital transmission. To protect the semantic information, an importance-aware OFDM transmission strategy is proposed to allocate the key features near the OFDM reference signals, where the feature importance is derived from the gradient-based method. At the receiver, the features are rematched with the shared codebook to further correct errors. Finally, experimental results demonstrate that our proposed scheme outperforms the conventional DeepSC and achieves better reconstruction performance under low SNR region.

title: Semantic-Aware Communications in Industrial IoT:What Can Be Tested Today, and What Is Missing?
authors: Rute C. Sofia
abstract: Classical networks treat every bit as equally important, which wastes time and energy in factories and requires extra traffic engineering for critical traffic. Semantic communications send only what a task needs, but how can they be tested under realistic conditions? This paper examines what can be tested today in 6G industrial IoT, that is, networks of factory machines, robots, and sensors, and what is still missing. It introduces semantic importance, a score attached to each message that states how much the message matters, and uses it in a context-driven design to derive eight testing needs. Existing simulators, emulators, testbeds, codecs, and learning frameworks are assessed against these needs, which reveals five gaps. We propose a toolchain of four components built around the ns-3 simulator for simulated and emulated scenarios.

title: An intent aware framework for semantic edge intelligence in autonomous 6g UAV and vehicular networks
authors: Salma Begum; Mudassir Khan; G. Suresh Babu; S Raghavi; Sapiah Binti Sakri
abstract: In autonomous communication between unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and vehicles in emerging sixth-generation (6G) networks, intelligent edge computing is essential for reliable decision-making under rapidly changing network conditions. This paper presents SEM-EDGE-X, a semantic edge intelligence framework integrating semantic feature extraction, Bayesian priority prediction, adaptive edge-to-cloud routing, semantic memory-assisted decision-making, dynamic resource management, adaptive cold-start semantic fusion, Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) validation, dynamic trust refinement, and Digital Twin simulation. Performance is evaluated using Python and SUMO mobility modelling with the KITTI and UAVDT datasets under varying channel conditions and network densities, in terms of semantic accuracy, simulated communication latency, throughput, energy consumption, scalability, computational cost, and robustness. The results indicate a favourable trade-off among communication efficiency, energy consumption, and semantic performance, with 95.76% semantic accuracy (transmission fidelity under channel noise, not correctness against ground-truth labels), approximately 1.04 ms simulated communication latency (propagation, transmission, and queueing only), throughput above 25 Mbps, and energy consumption below 0.006 mJ. The separately measured software execution time of the pipeline is approximately 109.6 ms and is not included in the simulated latency.

title: ParaJSCC: A Parameterized Framework for Reusable Multimodal Joint Source–Channel Coding
authors: Kemi Chen; Mingkai Chen; Youjia Chen; Qian Liu; Wei Gao; Tiesong Zhao
venue: ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM)
abstract: Multimodal signals, such as visual, audio, and tactile data, are increasingly maintained as persistent digital assets in immersive communication systems and digital twins. In these settings, the same multimodal content is repeatedly accessed by heterogeneous receivers with varying modality and bandwidth requirements. Existing compression and Joint Source-Channel Coding (JSCC) methods typically follow a per-request encoding paradigm, resulting in redundant computation and low efficiency during repeated access. To address this issue, we propose ParaJSCC, a multimodal JSCC framework designed for reusable representation serving. ParaJSCC converts each multimodal sample offline at the cloud/content server into a compact, quantized parameter package, which is then stored at the edge serving node for low-latency access. During serving, only the subset required by the current request is transmitted over the wireless channel, followed by lightweight decoding at the receiver. The framework employs a progressive shared-private parameterization to support modality-selective transmission and scalable reconstruction under varying bandwidth constraints. Experiments on multimodal datasets show that ParaJSCC significantly reduces online latency (e.g., from 17.18 ms to 4.34 ms for image-only requests and from 43.96 ms to 11.21 ms for full multimodal requests) and transmission rate (by 47.8%--51.2% for selective requests), while maintaining strong reconstruction quality under noisy channels.

title: QISFP: a quantum-inspired semantic fidelity protocol for energy-efficient and noise-resilient visual IoT transmission
authors: David Elias Emmanuel; Anil Fernando
abstract: Abstract Visual Internet of Things deployments operate under coupled bandwidth, energy and channel-reliability constraints, yet conventional video coding optimises pixel-level reconstruction rather than the preservation of task-relevant meaning. This paper presents QISFP, a quantum-inspired semantic fidelity protocol that treats semantic degradation as a stochastic state transformation rather than as additive signal distortion. It couples delta encoding of temporally associated object-level semantic states with a stochastic channel built from classical analogues of the depolarizing and amplitude-damping maps, and reconstructs meaning by energy- and confidence-weighted fusion over a temporal window. The framework is classical throughout: the quantum formalism supplies trace-preserving maps whose diagonal restriction is a stochastic matrix, which keeps per-object cost linear rather than quadratic in the semantic dimension. The induced class channel is shown to be $$M$$ M -ary symmetric, yielding two independent decay constants that characterise a semantic link and fix a multi-hop relaying budget, while a source-channel separation argument gives the attainability limit $$F \le 1 - p_d(1-1/M)$$ F ≤ 1 - p d ( 1 - 1 / M ) , met with equality by uncoded single-observation transmission; every attainable gain therefore lies in the temporal dimension. Simulation on CDNet 2014 and UCF-101 indicates 27.5% lower energy per frame and 30.3% lower transmitted volume than full-frame x264, with semantic fidelity of 0.922 against 0.855 for a frame-wise semantic baseline, at a cost of 1.28 dB in PSNR. An end-to-end measurement on detector output tests the theory directly: the frame-wise baseline tracks the single-use limit to within 0.022 IoU, the framework exceeds that limit wherever the channel is non-trivial, and at matched fidelity it requires between 42% and 64% fewer bits than the baseline. The protocol requires a few kilobytes of state and fewer than $$10^4$$ 10 4 operations per frame, so embedded feasibility is governed by the choice of semantic extractor rather than by QISFP itself.

title: Adaptive Channel Coding with Semantic-Aware Error Protection for 6G Non-Terrestrial Networks
authors: Ambar Bajpai
abstract: Abstract Non-terrestrial networks (NTNs) — comprising low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellites, high-altitude platform stations (HAPS), and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) — are increasingly regarded as a foundational layer of sixth-generation (6G) wireless systems, extending connectivity to rural, maritime, and disaster-affected regions that remain beyond the economic reach of terrestrial infrastructure. NTN links, however, present a uniquely hostile channel environment: long and time-varying propagation delay, large Doppler shifts induced by high relative platform velocity, deep fades from atmospheric and rain attenuation, and severe constraints on onboard power and computation. Conventional fixed-rate or classically-adaptive channel coding schemes, which react only to instantaneous signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), are poorly matched to this environment: they either over-provision redundancy, wasting scarce bandwidth and energy, or under-provision it and trigger the so-called cliff effect, in which a small SNR drop causes catastrophic decoding failure. In this paper we propose semantic-aware adaptive channel coding (SA-ACC), a framework that couples semantic importance estimation with rate- and redundancy-adaptive coding so that error-protection resources are allocated according to the task-relevant meaning of transmitted content rather than uniformly across all bits. We formalize the system model for a representative NTN scenario — a LEO downlink relayed through a HAPS node — define a semantic importance metric derived from task-gradient sensitivity, and design a two-stage adaptation control loop that jointly selects code rate, modulation order, and per-feature protection level under explicit delay and energy budgets. We further specify a complete evaluation methodology, comparing SA-ACC against fixed-rate LDPC/polar coding, conventional adaptive coding and modulation (ACM), and non-semantic deep joint source-channel coding (JSCC) across bit error rate, block error rate, semantic fidelity, throughput, latency, and energy metrics, and use this methodology to reason about SA-ACC’s expected behavior ahead of full numerical validation. Our architectural analysis indicates that SA-ACC should be able to sustain task-relevant reconstruction quality at lower effective SNR than baselines optimized purely at the bit level, at the cost of additional encoder and decoder complexity that we discuss explicitly. We close by outlining the simulation and ablation study required to convert this design-and-methodology contribution into a fully validated result.

title: Leakage-Aware Encrypted Semantic Communication with Key-Conditioned Signal Perturbation
authors: Omar Kaaki; Maria Slim; Mariette Awad; Hadi Sarieddeen
abstract: Encrypted semantic communication systems protect transmitted messages by inserting key-conditioned modules into a deep-learning semantic communication pipeline, but existing designs rely on a fixed adversarial weight and operate mainly at the semantic-feature level. We propose two changes to the encrypted semantic communication system (ESCS): a key-conditioned signal-domain perturbation layer, called learned adversarial perturbation injection (LAPI), and an information noise-contrastive estimation (InfoNCE)-guided adaptive training rule that {adds an adaptive leakage penalty alongside the fixed adversarial objective} using an InfoNCE-based proxy for mutual information leakage. Experiments on the Europarl corpus over additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) and Rayleigh fading channels show that InfoNCE-guided training is the primary source of eavesdropper suppression, reducing the eavesdropper's bilingual evaluation understudy (BLEU) score to approximately 0.07 at high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Adding LAPI to the InfoNCE-guided objective further lowers the InfoNCE-estimated leakage by 5-9% with low measured inference overhead, while its impact on legitimate-receiver BLEU depends on channel conditions. The two mechanisms operate on different parts of the pipeline and can be jointly applied.

title: Resource Allocation for Semantic‐Driven Multibeam Satellite Systems via Deep Reinforcement Learning
authors: Jianpeng Xu; Shuang Li; Xuehu Wang
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper focuses on resource allocation in a semantic‐driven multibeam geostationary earth orbit (GEO) satellite system. The sum semantic rate (SSR) is maximized by jointly designing the subchannel and power allocation, while satisfying the semantic similarity. Since the optimization problem is non‐convex and mathematically intractable, an algorithm based on deep reinforcement learning (DRL), specifically the softmax deep double deterministic policy gradients with prioritized experience replay (SD3‐PER) algorithm, is proposed to maximize the reward through sustained interaction with the semantic‐driven multibeam GEO satellite environment. Simulation findings demonstrate that the proposed scheme can achieve higher SSR than the benchmark algorithms.

title: Resource optimization for RIS-UAV integrated air-ground cooperative semantic communication driven by deep reinforcement learning
authors: Yufei Dai; Yuanyuan Yao; Sai Huang; Xinwei Yue
abstract: To meet the 6G semantic transmission requirements, this paper proposes an air-ground dual-mode semantic transmission architecture for Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface (RIS)-aided Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) networks. By dynamically assigning RIS-reflected links to users with long packets and direct UAV line-of-sight (LOS) links to users with short packets, we jointly optimize semantic symbols, RIS phase shifts, UAV three-dimensional (3D) trajectory, and transmit power to maximize the system-level semantic Quality of Experience (QoE). To efficiently solve the formulated non-convex mixed-integer optimization problem, we present an Action Space Decoupled Hybrid Deep Reinforcement Learning (ASD-HDRL) framework, which employs the Dueling Double Deep Q-Network (D3QN) for discrete semantic resource decision-making and Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) for continuous control optimization. Simulation results verify that the proposed ASD-HDRL achieves superior system-level semantic QoE performance.

title: Semantic SCL Decoding for Polar Codes
authors: Andy Huang; Chentao Yue; Branka S. Vucetic; Yonghui Li
abstract: Semantic error control coding (SECC) has emerged as a promising paradigm for improving communication reliability by exploiting the inherent structure and semantic dependencies of transmitted information. This paper proposes a semantic successive cancellation list (SCL) decoder for polar codes carrying natural-language text. A fine-tuned byte-level language model provides next-byte priors, which are converted into conditional bit costs and incorporated directly into the SCL path metric before each pruning step. This allows the decoder to jointly exploit channel reliability and source structure while retaining the conventional polar coding framework. The language model can also be invoked only for bytes whose channel decisions are unreliable, trading decoding performance for latency. Simulations for length-512 polar codes show substantial block error rate (BLER) improvements over conventional CRC-aided SCL (CA-SCL) decoding. At rate R=0.75 and list size L=16, the proposed decoder achieves more than 1 dB of gain in BLER compared to CA-SCL with the same L. Moreover, with L=8, it outperforms conventional CA-SCL with L=256 in terms of BLER, while requiring about one quarter of the decoding time of the latter in the evaluated software implementation.

title: QoE-Driven Hybrid Resource Allocation for Multi-User OFDMA Semantic Communications
authors: Xiaotian Xu; Zhifeng Tang; Guangchen Wang; Nan Yang; Xiangyun Zhou; Salman Durrani; Yansha Deng
abstract: In this paper, we develop a quality-of-experience (QoE)-driven hybrid resource allocation framework for multi-user downlink orthogonal frequency-division multiple access semantic communication systems, where the hybrid framework jointly handles continuous and discrete decision variables. Specifically, we formulate a mixed continuous-discrete optimization problem to jointly optimize transmit power, subcarrier allocation, and semantic decisions under coupled power and spectrum constraints. To better characterize semantic service quality, we propose a preference-inverse multiplicative exponential QoE that is bounded and non-compensatory, capturing the intrinsic ``both-required'' property of semantic rate and similarity. To solve the optimization problem, we develop a projection-based multi-agent deep deterministic policy gradient framework that enforces feasibility for continuous and discrete actions. Furthermore, we integrate Gumbel-softmax relaxation with an adaptive performance-driven temperature annealing scheme to enhance the learning of discrete semantic decisions. Simulation results demonstrate that our proposed framework achieves superior convergence, greater stability, and higher QoE compared to the conventional QoE design and penalty-based or fixed-temperature baselines, highlighting the benefits of our QoE design and the effectiveness of hybrid decision learning in semantic communications.

title: Data4Cyber: Labeled Cyber-Physical Datasets for Distribution-Grid Management Systems Under Representative OT Attacks
authors: Ömer Sen; Lennart Bader; Marawan Emara; Martin Serror; Benedikt Schwalm; Junichi Tsurumi; Tatsumi Oba; Tomohiro Izawa; Yoshihiro Ujiie
abstract: Cyberattacks against power systems increasingly exploit industrial communication and control dependencies arising from distributed energy resources (DER), remote management, and market-based incentives. Progress on intrusion detection is constrained by a lack of public datasets that align operational technology (OT) network telemetry with physical measurements and control context. Data4Cyber is a labeled cyber-physical dataset recorded in a laboratory distribution management system (DMS) for self-consumption optimization with photovoltaic generation, battery storage, controllable loads, and substation metering. It captures synchronized process measurements, controller context, price incentives, and packet captures (Modbus/TCP and MQTT) across one benign baseline and six attack scenarios spanning protocol-semantic Modbus manipulation, man-in-the-middle (MitM) false-data injection, and MQTT price manipulation. Its fixed 1 s time base, phase-resolved labels, and state-oriented representation support temporally blocked stateful-detector evaluation. Baseline results show that high recall alone is insufficient: several detectors achieve sensitivity through alarm saturation. Context-driven attacks require process-aware interpretation rather than single-channel thresholding.

title: Optimal Sampling and Transmission Policy for Information Freshness in Gossip Networks
authors: Irtiza Hasan; Ahmed Arafa
abstract: We study the optimal sampling and transmission policies for a transmitter communicating with n gossiping receivers with the objective of tracking a source's status over time using a semantic freshness metric: Version Age of Information (VAoI). The transmitter observes the version changes in the source, and can acquire a new information version by paying a sampling cost. The receivers gossip, allowing information exchange among each other without direct transmission. Gossiping can save on transmission cost, but it may propagate stale version information, necessitating transmitter intervention. With imperfect communication links, we formulate an infinite horizon average cost Markov Decision Process (MDP) in order to jointly optimize receivers' VAoIs, sampling and transmission costs in a time slotted fully connected (FC) gossip network. We first solve the MDP using Relative Value Iteration (RVI) algorithm. Then, we prove that the sampling decision has a threshold structure in the transmitter VAoI. Further, under reliable gossiping links, we show that transmission and idling has an VAoI-difference threshold structure with minimum VAoI activation. Numerical results obtained using RVI show that the optimal policy consistently outperforms natural baselines. These results characterize how source sampling, direct transmission, and receiver gossip should be jointly coordinated for cost-aware semantic freshness in gossip networks.

title: The Invisible Gap: Romanized Indic Generation Fails Where Automatic Metrics Succeed
authors: Madhu Sudhan Rao Beesetty; Surbhi Sharma; Devesh Maheshwari; Lokesh Meesala
abstract: Hundreds of millions of Indians communicate with digital systems in romanized Latin characters -- typing "aap kaise hain" rather than native script -- yet romanized Indic generation is absent from NLP benchmarks and evaluation frameworks. We demonstrate that automatic metrics (BGE-M3, BERTScore) systematically misrepresent the quality of romanized Hindi, Telugu, and Kannada generation. We evaluate four LLMs (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 2.5-flash, Qwen3.5-35B) on 142 OpenAssistant query-response pairs. On a 72-response diagnostic subset, native speakers rate GPT-5.5 1.43 points higher than Claude Opus 4.8 on a 12-point rubric, whereas their full-dataset BGE-M3 means differ by only 0.004. Two distinct model-specific failure modes emerge: Gemini produces script spillage (16.9% of Telugu responses leak native script), while Qwen collapses to English-only output (16.2% of Kannada responses). We introduce a failure-aware evaluation policy that assigns zero to empty outputs, script-corrupted responses, and instruction collapses -- revealing failures metrics alone cannot detect. Our results show that evaluating romanized Indic generation requires a coordinated bundle: semantic similarity, script compliance, failure coverage, and native-speaker acceptability.

title: Semantic Prior-Guided Incomplete Cross-Modal Retrieval with Noisy Labels
authors: Jiali Chen; Ruitao Pu; Yingke Chen; Dezhong Peng
abstract: Cross-modal retrieval (CMR) aims to bridge the semantic gaps between modalities by learning shared representations. Unfortunately, due to the dynamism and inconsistencies in real-world data acquisition, multimodal datasets frequently encounter severe modality incompleteness. Existing incomplete CMR methods adhere to a label-driven paradigm, relying heavily on categorical annotations as the semantic benchmark. However, label noise is difficult to avoid and often coexists with modality incompleteness. To address this challenge, we propose a novel semantic prior-guided framework for incomplete cross-modal retrieval with noisy labels, termed SPIRN. Specifically, SPIRN uses fixed semantic priors as a consistent reference for robust representation learning, noisy-label handling, and missing-modality completion. Based on this reference, Semantic Priors Guidance (SPG) establishes a stable category-level semantic space, Quality-aware Robust Learning (QRL) dynamically evaluates sample quality to distinguish clean samples from noisy ones and handles noise via reverse learning, Prior-guided Global Label Calibration (PGLC) rectifies corrupted annotations for refined supervision, and Confidence-driven Selective Imputation (CSI) recovers missing modalities from a cross-modal memory bank while filtering unreliable imputations with an increasing threshold. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first framework to jointly tackle the dual challenges of modality incompleteness and label noise in the CMR community. Extensive experiments on four widely used benchmark datasets demonstrate that SPIRN outperforms 11 state-of-the-art methods in various scenarios involving both missing modalities and noisy labels.

title: Token Importance-Aware Semantic Communication Enabled Robust Video Transmission
authors: Xiwen Zhang; Yubo Peng; Luping Xiang; Kun Yang
abstract: Video applications are increasingly prevalent, yet their high data volume and temporal dependency make robust wireless transmission challenging under limited communication resources. To address this issue, we propose a token importance-aware semantic communication (Ti-SemCom) framework for bandwidth-efficient video transmission. Specifically, object and motion information is jointly extracted to identify communication-relevant regions, which are hierarchically associated with semantic tokens according to their importance. The transmitted tokens are then dynamically selected based on both token importance and the available bandwidth, prioritizing more informative video content under resource constraints. At the receiver, untransmitted regions reuse recently reconstructed references to further reduce redundant transmission. Experiments on the CAVIAR dataset show that Ti-SemCom can achieve an 88.3\% reduction in communication cost while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality.

title: Constructing a Regional Slang Lexicon for Electricity Demands via Soft-Label Bidirectional Anchoring and Active Learning
authors: Rong Chang; Lijing Shi; Zhaoxiang Zang
abstract: Power-grid customer service increasingly relies on community social media, where customers describe outages, billing, and equipment faults in informal regional dialect. Such messages exhibit non-standard morphology, semantic drift, and out-of-vocabulary expressions that make manual lexicon construction costly and degrade conventional NLP tools. We propose a weak-supervision framework constructing a regional slang lexicon from curated dialect anchors and power-domain seed terms. Candidates are generated via Pointwise Mutual Information with soft-label bidirectional anchoring, retaining dialect-anchored terms while recording power-domain relevance as separate metadata, and are scored by combining Sentence-BERT semantic similarity with a jieba-based wordhood measure. Uncertainty-aware active learning with rule-based and retrieval-augmented LLM oracles is applied under three query strategies, and the resulting lexicon is evaluated by a higher-capability LLM calibrated against human expert annotations via Cohen's $κ$. On 11,177 real WeChat messages from Yuxi (Yunnan, China), the framework achieves an evaluator-estimated dialect precision of DP~$=$~1.0 with zero false positives. An ablation shows that soft-label layering retains 751\% more candidates than strict power-gating at identical precision, expanding the candidate pool from 41 to 349 terms. Human calibration ($n=46$) yields $κ_{\text{dialect}}=1.0$ and $κ_{\text{power}}=0.85$. The resulting 25--33-term lexicon, 4--5 of which are power-relevant, provides a preliminary resource for dialect-aware power-grid service NLP.

title: When Music Needs Meaning: Semantic Communication as a Transformative Enabler for the Musical Metaverse
authors: Ali Al Housseini; Jaime Llorca; Cristina Rottondi; Luca Turchet; Tiziano Leidi; Omran Ayoub
abstract: The Musical Metaverse (MM) enables geographically distributed musicians, audiences, sound engineers, and AI agents to interact through synchronized audio, visual, kinematic, and haptic streams, imposing latency, synchronization, bandwidth, and scalability requirements that are difficult to satisfy with conventional bit-level communication. This paper argues that semantic communication, understood here as the transmission of musically meaningful information rather than raw audio-visual-haptic samples, provides a principled communication paradigm for the MM. We define the MM from a communication perspective and derive modality-specific require ments; propose a three-pillar framework for musical semantic communication comprising semantics extraction, semantic-aware orchestration, and cross-modal semantic synchronization; survey representative work across semantic communication, music AI and edge orchestration, identifying the gaps that prevent their integration; and propose a semantic-first reference architecture based on device-side semantic encoders, edge semantic routers, and cross-modal semantic synchronization. The resulting framework positions the MM as a concrete and demanding use case for 6G semantic communication.

title: Triage models for surgical decision-making in patients with shoulder pain: an integrative review.
authors: Samah Hassan; Kenneth J Faber; Joy Christine MacDermid
abstract: Shoulder pain is a major cause of work absenteeism, affecting 1 in 3 adults. Although nonsurgical treatments like physical therapy are recommended as the first line of management, 40% of patients are referred for surgery before exploring these options. This review aimed to identify existing triage models used for shoulder pain referrals for surgery, guidelines for shoulder pain management that include criteria for surgical referral, and indications for surgery. An integrative review approach was used to comprehensively search major databases (Medline, PubMed, Embase, CINAHL Plus) and gray literature. Articles on triage models, referral processes, or surgery candidacy for shoulder pain were included. The searches retrieved 4510 articles, with 480 selected for full review and 71 articles included in this synthesis. Thirty-seven articles described various triage models and clinical decision-making processes for managing shoulder pain, including determining when to refer for surgical consultation and the indications for surgery. Seventeen articles compared surgical and nonsurgical treatments to identify surgical indicators, 10 articles examined factors affecting decision-making, and 7 articles explored predictor models for surgical outcomes. The findings underscore the need for a multifactorial decision-making process that acknowledges the complexity of pain within a biopsychosocial framework and incorporates patients' personal preferences into the triage decision-making process. These triage models should work across different contexts, eg, conservative, primary, and speciality care, to facilitate better patient experience across the continuum.

title: DecompJSCC: Joint Source-Channel Coding With Decoupled SNR and Rate Adaptation
authors: Yunhao Liu; Jiancun Fan; Haojun Sun; Jie Luo; Qing Zhao
abstract: Deep joint source-channel coding (DeepJSCC) for image transmission must adapt to changes in the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and available transmission resources. However, some existing joint-adaptive methods condition the encoder on the requested rate, while others apply static masks after encoding. The former couples latent formation to the rate request, whereas the latter cannot adapt channel selection to image content. To address these limitations, we propose DecompJSCC, which decomposes joint adaptation into SNR-conditioned latent formation and post-encoding rate control within a single model. The encoder applies SNR-conditioned block attention residuals across all stages, aggregating intra-stage and cross-stage semantic representations. At the receiver, an adapter performs SNR-conditioned affine correction. We introduce a post-encoding rate-adaptive channel semantic budgeting (RCSB) module whose shared gate selects channels of the formed latent by image content, adjusts their gains, and keeps exactly the requested count. This keeps the encoder output independent of the rate request for a fixed image and SNR. Experimental results show that DecompJSCC outperforms SwinJSCC and SA-RA-JSCC in peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) across a range of SNR and rate settings, by 0.64 and 1.00 dB over SwinJSCC and by 0.97 and 0.96 dB over SA-RA-JSCC on Kodak and CLIC2021, while using only 7.5% of SwinJSCC's Adaptive ModNet parameters.

title: ALMeD: Medieval French Gold-Standard
authors: Ragini Menon; Sabine Tittel
abstract: Medieval French is one of the Romance vernacular languages with a significant history of transmission and an enormous influence on other vernacular languages of the time. The sources convey valuable knowledge about all aspects of culture. The study of Medieval French has, over the last few years, increasingly benefited from NLP-based methods. There have been numerous efforts to parse medieval French; however, these efforts use corpora comprising legal texts and -- primarily -- literary texts as their foundation and training data. This means that, except for juridical resources, scientific literature is overlooked. We present ALMeD, an annotated, semantically rich corpus (work-in-progress) of medical and surgical treatises produced in medieval French, i.e., Old and Middle French, including Anglo-Norman. Our semantically disambiguated gold standard goes beyond existing resources, focusing on medical terminology, and accounts for morphological development, evolving syntactical structures and the lack of spelling normalisation in these languages.

title: STAR: Semantic-Criticality Tiered Allocation of Radio Resources via Zero-Shot Learning
authors: Albert Shaju; Christo Kurisummoottil Thomas; Mingzhe Chen
abstract: In remote inference, edge devices transmit high-resolution images over wireless links to a receiver, where an artificial intelligence (AI) model answers task-specific questions about these images to enable reliable decisions. These answers are often determined by a small set of task-causal pixels, such as those of text, whose corruption changes the answer, so these pixels must be delivered with high fidelity. Conventional transmission protects every pixel equally, so it either consumes many resource elements (REs) or corrupts these regions at low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). To overcome these limitations, in this paper, a zero-shot, domain-agnostic framework, termed semantic-criticality tiered allocation of resources (STAR), is proposed. In particular, a per-pixel semantic-criticality indicator (SCI) is derived from the attention of a frozen vision-language model, so new tasks and domains are handled by changing only the prompt, without retraining. The resulting task causality-aware resource allocation problem over protection tiers is solved exactly by a threshold rule on the SCI, realized by a coded tier for the task-causal pixels and an uncoded, downsampled base layer for the full image. Simulations over a 5G New Radio link demonstrate that STAR attains a semantic accuracy of at least 0.98 for $E_s/N_0 \geq -4$ dB and, at comparable semantic reliability, reduces the REs of robust coded transmission by 59.5% and 91.5% on factory- and vehicle-monitoring datasets, respectively, the latter without any change to the models. Although a deep joint source-channel coding baseline uses fewer REs at comparable semantic accuracy, it must be retrained with labeled data for every new task or domain.

title: One-Shot Federated Graph Learning via High-Fidelity Proxies and Transferability-Guided Collaboration
authors: Jia Jiang; Zihan Tan; Wenke Huang; Bin Yang; Mang Ye
abstract: One-shot Federated Graph Learning (OFGL) has emerged as a communication-efficient paradigm for federated graph learning under strict bandwidth constraints, compressing collaboration into a single transmission round. Nevertheless, this extreme setting suffers from a fundamental Single-Transmission Bottleneck, which limits both the quality and utility of exchanged knowledge. First, while existing methods attempt to distill private graphs into shareable proxies, their aggressive one-shot compression inherently triggers a fidelity crisis. This compression distorts local graph topology and semantics across clients, leading to externalized knowledge underexpression. Second, although the server aggregates these proxies to update global models, current integration schemes suffer from transferability agnosticism. The server cannot reliably identify cross-client collaboration potential, thus resulting in integrated knowledge underutilization. To tackle these dual challenges, we propose FedHFT, an effective One-Shot Personalized Federated Graph Learning (OPFGL) framework that addresses this bottleneck from two perspectives, namely High-Fidelity Knowledge Externalization and Transferability-Ware Knowledge Integration. We use Fidelity-Driven Proxy Refinement to preserve client-side knowledge fidelity, and Transferability-Steered Personalized Collaboration to enable adaptive server-side collaboration. The superiority of FedHFT is validated through extensive experiments on both homophilic and heterophilic graphs. The code is available at https://github.com/Jumpy-Juice/FedHFT.

title: SCALE: Real-Time Latent Communication for Cyber-Physical Agents
authors: Shanghao Shi; Jian Xiao; Ching-Hsiang Chan; Sanjoy Baruah; Sastry Kompella; Yevgeniy Vorobeychik; William Yeoh; Ning Zhang
abstract: Latent communication enables agents to collaborate efficiently by directly exchanging intermediate model representations rather than raw sensor data or text messages. Existing approaches, however, are primarily designed for LLM agents and do not consider the bandwidth constraints and heterogeneous task deadlines faced by cyber-physical agents. In this work, we propose SCALE, a real-time latent communication method tailored for cyber-physical agents. Motivated by the spatio-temporal continuity of the physical world, SCALE matches tokens across consecutive latent messages using similarity scores to identify reusable information and avoid redundant transmission. It then profiles the semantic gain and communication cost of transmitting different amounts of latent information. Based on these profiles, SCALE employs a real-time scheduler that jointly determines which pending messages to transmit and how many latent tokens to send, subject to available bandwidth and task deadlines. We evaluate SCALE across three cyber-physical benchmarks and a physical spider robot case study under diverse network conditions and heterogeneous task deadlines. Our results show that SCALE significantly improves both task performance and on-time delivery in bandwidth-constrained networks. Our code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SCALE-4E80/.

title: English as a Foreign Language Instructors’ Professional Identity and Professional Development in Higher Education Institutions
authors: Hijjatul Qamariah
venue: SZTE Repository of Dissertations (University of Szeged)
abstract: Teacher Professional identity (TPI) and professional development (PD) are key constructs for the quality of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) instruction in higher education. However, research in non Western contexts often lacks conceptual clarity and methodological depth in explaining how these constructs emerge and interact. Guided by a sociocultural perspective that views identity as socially constructed, negotiated, and shaped through participation in institutional practices, this study examines how Indonesian EFL instructors construct their professional identities and how these identities influence their teaching practice and engagement in professional development. An exploratory sequential mixed methods design was employed. The qualitative phase involved semi structured interviews (N = 10) and ego centered network cards (N = 11) to capture instructors’ lived experiences and the relational influences shaping their identities. Thematic analysis identified five themes: professional identity construction, professional development practices, pedagogical agency, institutional influence, emotional and relational dimensions. These themes informed the development of a survey instrument, which was validated and administered to 161 instructors across diverse higher education institutions. The quantitative phase used correlation analysis to examine associations among validated constructs: teaching practice, pedagogical knowledge, reflective practice, institutional support, and professional development. This was followed by multiple regression analyses to determine the extent to which TPI predicted these outcomes. The results showed strong correlations among all constructs. Multiple regression analysis showed that mentorship emerged as the strongest predictor (β = .473, p < .001), indicating that instructors who receive meaningful guidance and peer support tend to report stronger professional identities. Self directed learning also significantly predicted identity strength (β = .395, p < .001), suggesting that instructors who actively engage in autonomous learning and skill development tend to construct stronger professional identities. Institutional support also contributed significantly (β = .344, p < .001), demonstrating that supportive institutional contexts foster stronger professional identity formation. Teaching experience was not a significant predictor of professional identity (β = .026, p = .336), suggesting the accumulation of teaching experience alone does s not automatically result in a more developed professional identity. Regression analysis further showed that PI significantly predicted teaching practice and engagement in PD, suggesting that identity plays a substantial role in shaping professional behavior rather than merely reflecting accumulated experience. While professional development contributes to identity formation, the findings suggest that identity exerts a stronger influence on instructors’ developmental choices and instructional decisions, pointing to a reciprocal but asymmetrical relationship. This study contributes to the field in three main ways: (1) by offering a contextually grounded conceptualization of EFL instructor identity in Indonesian higher education; (2) by providing a validated measurement instrument that may support future research and policy-related work and (3) by presenting empirical evidence of the important role of identity in shaping teaching practice and sustained professional development. The findings underscore the importance of institutional environments that recognize the dynamic nature of teacher identity and provide meaningful, long term support for professional growth.

title: Dream-Butterfly: Configuring Embodied Conversational Guidance for Public Outdoor Mixed Reality Exhibitions
authors: Dongyijie Primo Pan; Shuyue Li; Yawei Zhao; Junkun Long; Hao Li; Pan Hui
venue: ACM Symposium on Virtual Reality Software and Technology (VRST)
abstract: Public outdoor mixed reality (MR) exhibitions make guidance a spatial interaction problem: visitors need timely explanations while roaming open sites, attending to virtual artworks, hazards, bystanders, and route choices. We present Dream-Butterfly, a field-deployed embodied conversational guide for campus-scale outdoor MR exhibitions. Visitors explicitly summon the lightweight non-humanoid guide; it returns visibly to a hand-relative dialogue position and answers using retrieval-augmented responses scoped by the MR runtime to the artwork currently encountered. Within the resulting mixed guidance ecology, staff remain accountable for safety, wayfinding, device support, and contingencies. Dream-Butterfly was deployed with over 30 spatially anchored artworks across a 26,000 m2 campus site, which we use as a stress case for public MR guidance under walking, field-of-view limits, route choice, bystander exposure, and safety constraints. In an in-the-wild study with 24 visitors, we compared two role arrangements: agent-default, where the embodied guide served as the default channel for artwork interpretation, and docent-default, where staff provided primary narration while the agent remained optional. Agent-default guidance was associated with more available, visitor-timed explanations, higher immersion/engagement, and stronger hedonic quality, while increasing visitors’ self-curation burden around pacing, attention management, and question formulation. We argue that making interpretation available at visitors’ chosen moments improves the timing of explanation in outdoor MR and shifts more work to visitors: deciding when to stop, what to ask, how deeply to engage, and when to move on.

title: FlexMARL: Graph-Driven Rollout-Training Co-Design for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
authors: Zhida Jiang; Zhaolong Xing; Jiawei Lu; Yipei Niu; Qingyuan Sang; Liangxu Zhang; Wenquan Dai; Junhua Shu; Jiaxing Wang; Qiangyu Pei; Qiong Chen; Xinyu Liu; Fangming Liu; Han Ai; Zhen Chen; Ke Zhang
abstract: Despite algorithm-level innovations for multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), the underlying infrastructure for large-scale MARL remains underexplored. Existing training frameworks primarily optimize for single-agent scenarios and fail to capture the graph-structured nature of MARL. This fundamental mismatch leads to three MARL-specific challenges: topology-induced rollout skew, critical path synchronization barriers, and dynamic training demand. To bridge this gap, we propose FlexMARL, a graph-driven rollout-training co-designed framework for large-scale LLM-based MARL. FlexMARL introduces the multi-agent execution graph (MEG) and materializes the intermediate representation as the MEG Store, which provides decentralized multi-table storage and serves as the data hub for system components. Built around the MEG Store, the Rollout Engine develops dependency parallel sampling with hierarchical load balancing, which reduces inference latency and balances intra-agent/inter-agent loads. The Joint Orchestrator exploits an agent-level asynchronous pipeline to mitigate the critical path synchronization barriers while maintaining consistency. The Training Engine achieves on-demand resource allocation by collectively managing training processes for individual agents. The training states of different agents are swapped via location-agnostic communication APIs. Empirical results on a production cluster demonstrate that FlexMARL achieves up to 7.3x speedup and improves hardware utilization by up to 5.6x compared to existing frameworks.

title: Modelling the drivers of modular construction adoption in Australia: a hybrid interpretive and classification approach
authors: Ayaz Khan; Mohammed A. Aloshan
abstract: Modular construction (MC) is increasingly promoted in Australia as a pathway toward more sustainable and efficient building delivery; however, adoption remains limited because the conditions shaping implementation are not yet fully understood. Existing studies largely identify or rank adoption drivers independently, with limited integration of hierarchical structural modelling and data-driven classification in the Australian context. This study investigates drivers of MC uptake through a mixed-method approach integrating qualitative evidence with quantitative modelling. A targeted literature scan and semi-structured interviews with 15 professionals, 11 based in Australia and four New Zealand-based comparative experts produced and refined an inventory of 79 drivers. Interview-occurrence analysis and category-specific Pareto evaluation prioritised the drivers; TISM-MICMAC modelled relationships among eight categories; and an ANN assessed how consistently occurrence and structural attributes reproduced the Pareto-defined classification. Social, technological, and supply-chain considerations occupied the strongest structural positions. A five-member content-review panel drawn from the remaining survey volunteer pool provided favourable ratings on 27 of 30 item responses (90%), with item-level favourable proportions of 60–100%. This supports face and content credibility only. Because the framework was developed from one small purposive dataset and the classifier target was occurrence-derived, the computational results remain internal-consistency evidence rather than independent causal or predictive validation.

title: Uncertainty Quantification for Financial Foundation Models: A Survey
authors: Mingjun Sun; Zijie Zhao; Shenbo Xu
venue: ACM International Conference on AI in Finance (ICAIF)
abstract: Financial foundation models increasingly support workflows spanning financial question answering, disclosure analysis, forecasting, and decision-making. In these settings, uncertainty may concern whether evidence is valid and available at the relevant time, whether an interpretation is justified, which outcomes remain plausible, or which action is preferred under costs and risk constraints. Because these objects arise at different points in a workflow, uncertainty cannot be reduced to confidence in a final output. We introduce a source-aware framework that distinguishes six sources of uncertainty across evidence and context, model and inference, and outcome and action, while treating agentic workflows as the execution layer through which uncertainty can propagate, change form, or be reduced. We develop a mechanism-based taxonomy grounded in how methods construct or verify uncertainty and reliability representations, and use it to assess their applicability across financial task domains. We further map finance-specific empirical studies across the taxonomy and task domains to characterize the current research landscape. Our analysis shows that most reviewed studies address uncertainty in individual parts of financial workflows, with limited work connecting evidence and reasoning reliability to downstream prediction and constrained action. By connecting where uncertainty arises, how it is represented, and how it bears on downstream decisions, this survey provides a unified foundation for studying and evaluating uncertainty in financial foundation models.

title: NosRacer: Dynamic Detection of Race Conditions in On-Device Network Operating Systems
authors: Runze Wu; Jingbo Zhai; Shanming Ping; Lingzhi Ouyang; Hua Duana; Qin Zou; Chengcheng Huang; Bingshe Liu; Xudong Lang; Xiaoxing Ma; Yu Huang
abstract: Commercial on-device network operating systems (NOSes) run the complex control planes of production routers and switches, where configuration update tasks are executed by multiple loosely coupled components through asynchronous message passing. Such executions are prone to race conditions: the same ordered input commands may produce different outcomes when messages are delivered in different orders. The race conditions are difficult to expose because they often manifest only as subtle, delayed malfunctions. Existing static analysis techniques lack scalability and precision for large-scale industrial NOSes, while dynamic ones incur substantial system-execution cost when attempting to cover the space of asynchronous message interleavings. To address the challenges above, we present NosRacer, a dynamic analysis framework for race condition detection in industrial-grade on-device NOSes. NosRacer uses a two-phase design. The concentration phase reduces analysis scope by leveraging the locality of configuration update tasks. Race condition detection is then limited to a small subset of involved components and crucial state variables, thereby reducing the detection cost. The perturbation phase proactively perturbs message asynchrony to increase the likelihood of executions with race-condition-exposing message interleavings. It keeps perturbation practical by grouping compatible perturbations for parallel execution and adaptively strengthening perturbations. We implement NosRacer in a commercial, actively developed NOS. NosRacer is integrated into the existing testing factory and used to detect race conditions in 5 key control-plane components. NosRacer achieves 66% precision and detects 21 race conditions confirmed by developers as severe bugs, while keeping the detection overhead below 10%.

title: ATLAS: Expert-Guided Sustainable Satellite Backhaul for Off-Grid Wildlife Monitoring
authors: Hao Fang; Miao Zhang; Haoyuan Zhao; Long Chen; Yi Ching Chou; Chi Xu; Cheng Pan; Jiangchuan Liu
abstract: Remote wildlife monitoring increasingly depends on high-fidelity cameras and sensors deployed far from grid power and terrestrial networks. Low Earth orbit satellite links can provide connectivity in these settings, but their high power draw and variable bandwidth, combined with intermittent on-site solar harvesting, make continuous backhaul infeasible. Current systems therefore filter at the edge, with motion triggers that waste limited energy and bandwidth on environmental artifacts, or fixed vision models that cannot follow evolving expert objectives. We present \textsc{ATLAS}, an expert-guided edge-to-cloud system that treats satellite backhaul as a scarce resource for off-grid wildlife monitoring. \textsc{ATLAS} uses foundation models to compile natural-language expert intent into semantic scoring logic, combines semantic relevance with environmental and energy state, and uses a constrained reinforcement-learning scheduler to decide which clips to upload and when. As a representative case study, we deployed \textsc{ATLAS} for over six months across 18 off-grid salmon-monitoring river sites. \textsc{ATLAS} achieves a mean clip-selection accuracy of $87.4\%$, exceeding mean baseline accuracy by $26.4$ percentage points, while maintaining near-continuous operation through low-solar periods in which baselines incur 16.0\% downtime.

title: Understanding Contextual Bias in Agricultural CNNs Through Hidden-Neuron Concept Induction
authors: Abhilekha Dalal; Avishek Das; Samatha Ereshi Akkamahadevi
abstract: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) can classify images using background-dominated patches that contain little or none of the target object, showing that they exploit contextual information. Previous studies detected this behavior through classification accuracy but say little about what CNN hidden layers represent. We investigate whether Concept Induction can reveal interpretable visual properties associated with hidden-neuron activations on contextual image patches. Using five agricultural datasets with high, moderate, and low contextual bias, we analyze four CNN architectures at three network depths and five patch locations. Quantitative image descriptors of each patch are encoded in a knowledge graph and used as background knowledge for Concept Induction, which derives logical expressions characterizing neuron activation. These expressions are tested on held-out images using the Mann-Whitney U test and Cliff's delta. Of 48,013 tested neuron-feature pairs, 13,164 (27.4%) were validated. Validation was most frequent at intermediate depths (mean 40.2% at mid layers versus 12.0% at deep layers), and no patch location dominated across datasets. Among the tested descriptors, edge, Gabor, and Tamura texture features had the highest validation rates. Stronger contextual bias did not correspond to higher neuron-feature validation rates: moderately biased Sugarcane had the highest rate (40.5%) and highly biased Cassava the lowest (19.2%). These results suggest that behavioral context dependence and the semantic interpretability of hidden neurons capture different aspects of CNN behavior, and that Concept Induction can complement patch-based bias detection.

title: RecMem: Recurrent Memory Compression for Long-Sequence Generative Recommendation
authors: Haoyi Hu; Gaoyang Guo; Yunjia Xi; Wen Chen; Weiwen Liu; Jian Wu; Yuning Jiang; Weinan Zhang
abstract: Generative recommendation benefits from long interaction histories, but the cost of processing them directly grows with history length. We propose RecMem, a recurrent memory compression framework guided by three desiderata: space invariance, semantic fidelity, and lifelong evolvability. RecMem compresses historical segments into a fixed set of memory slots using a bifurcated encoder-decoder with shared lower layers and slot-wise forget-gated updates. Recommendation supervision trains the memory to preserve predictive information, while stream-consistency training aligns predictions from sequential and packed processing. By construction, the memory state and decoder context are independent of history length; under contraction and approximate semigroup consistency, we further derive a horizon-independent bound on the state discrepancy between these two processing orders. On MerRec, RecMem uses 16 memory slots and a 216-token decoder context, compared with 1,200 tokens for HSTU-1200, while retaining 87.9% of HSTU-1200's Recall@10 and 97.0% of its Recall@200. It outperforms PHSTU and the evaluated recent-only and retrieval baselines, and analyses of distant history show that archived interactions contribute predictive signal.

title: Vision-Language Models Reproduce a Human Mental-Extrapolation Bias in the Watanabe Illusion
authors: Eiji Watanabe; Kyohei Ueda; Kagayaki Kato; Masaki Watabe; Akiyoshi Kitaoka
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used for visual judgments, yet whether they share human perceptual biases, and where in the model such biases arise, is unclear. We addressed this with the Watanabe Illusion, a stimulus not previously studied quantitatively: an oblique segment inside a circle whose extension geometrically hits the topmost of 11 dots, yet human observers (n = 131) reported a dot near the middle of the column. Five VLMs (Qwen2.5-VL-32B and 7B, Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.5 Instant, Gemini 3.5 Flash), given the identical stimulus and wording, all deviated in the same direction. In the open-weight Qwen2.5-VL-32B, linear probes on the vision encoder recovered the line angle and the target dot six to eight times more accurately than its behavioral responses. A layer-wise logit lens showed that the correct answer dominates in the middle layers of the language model and is overwritten in late layers only under a visual-judgment frame. Naming the illusion, requesting suppression of prior knowledge, forcing a visual chain of thought, and 390 semantic preambles left the response center unchanged; only disclosing the correct answer moved it. VLMs may therefore carry human perceptual biases at the language-generation stage, where they resist declarative correction.

title: S1Pert: Scalable Target-Specific Gene Response Prediction with System-One Intelligence
authors: Xiaoqi Sheng; Hou wang; Yan Liang; Yutong Li; Wenhao Du; Tinghe Zhang; Jiawen Liu; Hongmin Cai
abstract: Predicting transcriptional responses to unseen genetic perturbations is essential for extending CRISPR screens across vast target--gene combinations. However, models can achieve strong aggregate predictive performance by reproducing historical gene-level response frequencies without adequately distinguishing the effects of different perturbations. Reliable prediction at the transcriptome scale is further challenged by uncertain response labels and redundant computation across millions of target--gene pairs. We present S1Pert, a System-One framework for target-specific gene response prediction with non-autoregressive online inference. S1Pert combines directional Welch tests and equivalence testing to distinguish statistically supported responses from inconclusive observations. A frozen System-One encoder extracts reusable semantic representations of perturbation targets, query genes, and historical evidence. Compact pair-specific interactions are then computed and cached offline. A lightweight hierarchical cross-attention decoder integrates these representations with cross-target pairwise ranking and synchronized historical-evidence dropout to reduce reliance on gene-level response frequencies. Extensive experiments demonstrate that S1Pert improves target-specific response discrimination while maintaining reliable prediction and efficient inference across diverse cellular contexts. These findings highlight the potential of System-One decision learning for scalable perturbation-response prediction beyond historical gene-level response tendencies. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/liujiawen-jpg/S1Pert.

title: What Do Multilingual Self-Supervised Speech Encoders Know About Sentence Meaning?
authors: Kevin Krahn; Eric Fosler-Lussier
abstract: Self-supervised speech models (S3Ms) have been scaled up to thousands of languages and millions of hours of audio, yet little is known about how these models structure semantic knowledge across languages. In this work, we probe sentence-level semantics in massively multilingual S3Ms across 76 languages, using linear maps from frozen speech representations into a frozen text embedding space, evaluated by cross-modal retrieval. Sentence meaning is linearly accessible but highly uneven across languages and resource tiers. Cross-lingual probes can match language-specific probes on languages never seen in probe training, but per-model monolingual decodability does not predict transfer. Within the OmniASR wav2vec family, scaling from 300M--7B disproportionately benefits high-resource languages, and ASR tuning sharply improves semantic decodability while making representations more language-specific. However, semantic content is entangled with acoustics, inflating apparent performance on single-speaker corpora.
